candidates.title: GPT-6.1 Terra brings lower-cost computer use to the API
candidates.summary: OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra in the API, ChatGPT Work and Codex with computer use, visual reasoning and lower standard API prices than GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol.
candidates.what_changed: The new gpt-6.1-terra model became available at $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens and $5 per million output tokens; OpenAI also published a safety-card addendum and first-party evaluation results.
candidates.why_it_matters: Developers now have a materially cheaper model option for high-volume visual and computer-use workflows, but its benchmark, factuality and safety claims remain first-party.
candidates.engineer_takeaway: Re-evaluate routing for visual and computer-use tasks against your own acceptance tests, latency and total task cost; do not treat vendor benchmarks as production guarantees.

evidence.rationale: Launch, pricing, availability and safety-card evidence are first-party OpenAI publications.
evidence.independent_validation: No independent production comparison was identified in the frozen window.
evidence.claim_scope: Performance, factuality, safety and cost-per-task comparisons are OpenAI evaluations; only availability and posted prices are treated as established here.

signal.rationale: A broadly available lower-cost computer-use model changes practical routing and automation choices.

learning_gap.existing_explainer_status: Explain why per-token price and vendor benchmark scores do not establish production cost.

deduplication.canonical_event: OpenAI releases GPT-6.1 Terra with API, Work and Codex availability and posted prices.
deduplication.previous_coverage: No matching URL, model-release event or story filename was found in the indexed repository archive through main 3ab499b; latest daily stories stop at October 26 and cover different events.
deduplication.material_delta: A new model and price point became available.

candidates.title: Meta enforces internal-agent data rules at the access boundary
candidates.summary: Meta described PrivacyLib, a common client-side privacy layer that observes or blocks data accesses across many internal systems, including supported internal-agent tool-call paths.
candidates.what_changed: Meta disclosed how AgentLib propagates agent session and tool-call context through supported paths to PrivacyLib, where policy modules can observe or deny access at the data boundary; the company reports billions of checks per second.
candidates.why_it_matters: The design moves agent authorization away from trusting the model or tool wrapper and toward enforceable policy at the system that owns the data.
candidates.engineer_takeaway: Propagate caller and session context to stable data boundaries, keep enforcement separate from observation, simulate policy changes, and make rollback local to each module.

evidence.rationale: Meta's engineering team provides implementation details, scale claims, code examples and stated limitations.
evidence.independent_validation: No independent audit of coverage, latency or enforcement correctness was identified.
evidence.claim_scope: Architecture and scale are company-reported; unsupported paths, external products and universal policy completeness are not claimed.

signal.rationale: The disclosed pattern directly addresses dynamic agent access with enforceable controls at the data boundary.

learning_gap.existing_explainer_status: Contrast model/tool-level approvals with data-boundary enforcement.

deduplication.canonical_event: Meta discloses PrivacyLib integration for observing and enforcing supported internal-agent data accesses.
deduplication.previous_coverage: No matching URL, PrivacyLib name or agent data-boundary event was found in repository code search or story filenames through pinned main.
deduplication.material_delta: A concrete production architecture for agent context propagation and data-boundary enforcement is disclosed.
